utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, very much. I would like to greet the Prosecution, the Defence counsel. I'd like to greet the accused as well. I can see that two of them are not here today because they have not recovered, and I wish them the best. I also greet everyone else in this courtroom. I'm first going to give the floor to the registrar because I need two IC numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. 3D has submitted a list of objections to documents tendered by the OTP through Witness Salem Cerenic. This list shall be given Exhibit number IC 499. OTP has also submitted a list, and that's a response to the Defence objections regarding OTP exhibits tendered through Witness L, and it shall be given the Exhibit number IC 500. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. A few points. First of all, the Chamber has reviewed the issues that the parties want to raise during the hearing tomorrow, both the Prosecution and the Defence have notified us of the issues they want to be discussed tomorrow. We've reviewed these submissions, and we have decided upon an agenda with the -- most of the issues raised by the parties. We believe that some of the issues that are pending before the Appeals Chamber should not be discussed tomorrow. The Trial Chamber's legal officer will hand out the agenda once we've completed the testimony of the witness. The agenda has been set by the Trial Chamber, and tomorrow we'll first give the floor to the Prosecution followed by the Defence, and you will have the amount of time I mentioned yesterday. That was the first point. Second point: The Trial Chamber has considered the matter of the certification of the appeal, and it's going to issue a decision about this. It's an appeal following the decision by the Appeals Chamber in its majority. The Trial Chamber believed that the Appeals Chamber was seized of the matter and therefore that there was no need to rule on the request for certification, but alternatively the Trial Chamber in its majority would have granted certification. As far as I'm concerned, I'm going to deliver a dissenting opinion about these two points and this will be circulated as well. Third point: Yesterday Ms. Alaburic put a number of questions to the witness, and whilst doing so she was invited by my colleague, my fellow Judge, to ask a question again because there might have been some doubts about what had been said. I would like to draw your attention, and I'm talking to everyone, that when you ask a question you should not speak too fast, because the interpreters, who are doing a tremendous job, find it sometimes difficult to follow us because we just speak too fast, and this can lead to mistakes in the interpretation, and this can have an impact on the understanding we have of the proceedings. Judge Prandler several times reminded you of this, and I should remind you of this as well. Why? Because on the basis of very serious studies conducted in the field of interpretation, as a general rule when you are -- when you talk about simultaneous interpretation, only 90 per cent of the words we speak, we utter, can be rendered by the interpreter, but amongst these studies carried out in the field of interpretation it appears that the meaning of a sentence can be rendered only at a level of 80 per cent. Therefore, there is a margin of error, and that margin of error, we can reduce it if we speak more slowly. I must say myself that I -- sometimes I'm a culprit, I speak too fast, so I'll try to speak more slowly from now on. And I would like to invite each and every one of us to follow suit, because we do not want to be confronted with a situation where we believed that we understood something and it was not actually what was being said. Thus the proceedings will be more serene from now on. That's a point I wanted to make before you. Let me add that apparently, but that's subject to some research that should be conducted, and I can't do it myself, but apparently we have already produced 16.000 pages of transcripts, ever since the beginning of this trial, and if we follow that rhythm, that pace, considering what's left of the Prosecution case, we have an estimate, it might not be accurate, but for what it's worth, we could have a total at the end of 50.000 pages of transcript. In the history of this Tribunal, this will be an absolute record. And it might even be a record in the history of international justice, 50.000 pages of transcript apparently. But, of course, some research should be done into the matter, but apparently ever since we've begun these proceedings, this trial, because of our speed we produce 20 per cent more pages of transcript than an average trial if you have -- you have the average trial X producing 100 pages of transcript, we produce 120 pages in this trial. So if we compare this trial to all the other trials ever heard in this institution, apparently we produce 20 more -- 20 per cent more pages of transcript, an added value of 20 per cent. That's some food for thought, I believe, and we might have the opportunity later on to reflect on this issue again. I'm going to ask the usher to bring in the witness. Let me add that we will have 10 minutes of questions for this witness by Ms. Tomic, but -- unless Ms. Alaburic has not finished. Did you still want to ask questions, Ms. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to say good afternoon, and my answer is that I have not concluded the cross-examination. I have a few very short questions remaining which will take me a maximum of 10 minutes, and that will round off what I wanted to ask the witness about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Good afternoon, sir. Good afternoon on behalf of everyone of here in the courtroom. We'll complete your testimony today. There's still one Defence counsel who wants to put a number of questions to you, and then a second one. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon. We're just going to have a very brief discussion and then that will complete my part of the cross-examination. Mr. Likic, you told us yesterday that you were unemployed. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, do you receive any remuneration as a member of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I receive 33 convertible marks.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, when you tabled this request for assistance and remuneration, what period of time did you stipulate as having spent in the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You sent in a request for this remuneration of 33 marks; is that right? You had to write a request?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't write a request for 33 marks, but I did write a request.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Now, in that request what did you say? How long were you a member of the BH army? How long did you spend in the BH army? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- well, I can't remember now, but I do know very well that I was there from the 13th of January, 1994, to the end. I was even for a month, a small period -- a short period of time I was even in the active -- well, what was it called? This army, the army that gets money now, the professional one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I asked you what you wrote down in your request. Did you write the duration of the time you spent in the BH army? When did you become a BH army member, from what time?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said -- I wrote down -- well, I asked for invalidity remuneration.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me help you out here. In your request did you stipulate that in 1993 you were a member of the BH army as well?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, may we show the witness a document that I have prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could Their Honours be handed over copies too? The document is a long one, but we're just going to spend a very short period of time on it, just to go through two or three important questions with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Likic, you told us that not a single man came to Stupni Do at around the 20th of October, 1993, as reinforcement to the defence of Stupni Do. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes. You said that yesterday, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in the document that you have before you, it is analysis of the implementation of tasks and assignments of the Vares operation with the chronology of events, which was issued by the command of the Operative Group East, Istok, TG tactical group Vares 6th Corps of the BH army. Would you take a look at page 6. In the English version it is on page 5, and the sticker marks page 5. May we have the English text on the ELMO please. Thank you. So in the middle of page 6 in the official report it says, referring to Stupni Do that links with severed with the unit at Stupni Do, and then it says in brackets "With a reinforced platoon numbering 39 men which defended Stupni Do." So from that sentence it would emerge that in Stupni Do there was a unit of the BH army which was reinforced with a platoon of 39 men, and that they together defended Stupni Do. Now, do you have any knowledge about the fact that Stupni Do was defended in this way no. As far as I know, and as far as what people said, because I wasn't there to know myself, it's the 23rd, I was in the camp, so after that the stories going round of the people who survived, they said that nobody came in from outside. No soldiers from outside came to Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'll tell you what this document is about. It was the only document that I was going to use, but it is document 4D 00519. 4D 00519. Now, may I conclude, Witness, that from later statements by your compatriots you came to the conclusion that there were no reinforcements coming into the BH army in Stupni Do. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, tell us, do you have any knowledge whatsoever about how the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina planned to take control of Vares? And that is a document that you have in front of you. Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please believe me when I say I don't. I really know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm going to ask you just one more question. You said that after you were incarcerated you were interrogated about the military situation in Stupni Do; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your written statement it says, in fact, that the HVO soldiers were exclusively interested in learning what the military situation was in Stupni Do; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, now, this interest on the part of the HVO soldiers, does it relate to the days when you were arrested on the 18th, and then further on the 19th, 20th and 21st of October, 1993? Is that what it relates to?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't understood you again.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You were arrested on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And my question is whether the interrogation about the military situation in Stupni Do was interesting to the members of the HVO who were questioning you already then, on the 18th, and in the days that followed after that, or sometime later?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were taken into custody, when we were arrested, they interrogated us that first night, asking us questions about Stupni Do, and then that questioning went on when the foreigners turned up, or people from other places. They questioned us again. So they took us out. They interrogated me, and they took us out one by one.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us, did you wonder yourself why HVO members were interested in the situation in Stupni Do? Did you ever ask yourself that, why they were interested on the 18th of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what can you tell us? Why were they interested in that?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said earlier on what I heard from Esref and Himza, that that's what they expected. They expected that they might be attacked, that the village might be attacked, because we were together in the cell. We didn't go out to be interrogated together, but we were in the cell together and so we discussed this matter amongst ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, since you are from Stupni Do yourself, let me ask you this: To the best of your knowledge, the BH army, can it launch an attack on Vares from the axis and direction of Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why? Why not?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Stupni Do was -- I said earlier on it was encircled from all sides. On one side you had the Serb forces, and on the other side round about, all round -- all around the other sides were the Croatian forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: May I just ask you a direct question? What place is between Stupni Do on the road to Vares, on that route? Was there a place in between Stupni Do and Vares?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Alaburic. Ms. Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, sir, yesterday when you looked at the list, when you were looking at the list of the camp inmates from -- by the association of inmates, the 23rd of October, you recognised one of the names. Salem Cerenic was one of those names that you recognised, and you said that was a person that was taken together with you from the school in that group of 25 persons to Majdan; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tomic, can you please speak closer to the microphone. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: On the 19th of March we questioned Mr. Cerenic here, and he talked about those events. However, there are certain parts that lack clarity or some of the things he said in describing the situation are different to what you say in your statement, and I think they're essential points. So I'll go through them slowly with you, and I'm not going to tell you what Mr. Cerenic said, not to waste time. We all have the transcript and can read it, and I'll give the transcript pages. But tell me this: According to your statement you were taken to Majdan from the secondary school in Vares; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: My next question is --

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it's not correct. We were taken from the elementary school. Not the secondary school, the elementary school called Vladimir Nazor in Vares.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: So what you say in your statement is not correct, because there it says that you were taken from the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the elementary school or primary school.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: My next question is this: In your statement you say that you were taken to the steelworks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: You stand by that, that it was the steelworks?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement further on you say that you were guarded there by two civilian policemen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question: In your statement you said that in that group of 25, after you were taken to the steelworks, that you were -- the physical abuse continued, and you described the events with the two soldiers who introduced themselves as being Serbs; not to go into a description of the whole incident, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. I'd just like to point out the statement by Mr. Cerenic of the 19th of March -- or, rather, his testimony in the direct -- in the examination-in-chief where he describes the events in Majdan. I don't want to repeat it all, his testimony, but it was a different location, different conditions, different guards than the ones this witness described, and Mr. Cerenic repeated in the cross-examination when I was asking him, and that is page 15.944, lines 7 to 9, and I have to further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Ibrisimovic, I believe you have no questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for me, I only have one question to put to you, but before doing so I would like to thank Ms. Alaburic for having highlighted the sentence in English in the relevant documents, because thus we can immediately identify the passage the question is related to. I'd like to invite the other counsel to do the same in the future, because thus we gain time and it's a very useful way of going about it. Sir, I had the following question for you: Ms. Alaburic asked you repeatedly when you were a member of the ABiH. You replied that that was not the case, that you became a member only as of January 1994. At some point I believe that Ms. Alaburic would submit a document, wherein your record of service it is stated that you were a member of the ABiH starting 1993. Since the document was not produced, I'm not going to deal with it. However, page 7, line 19 of the transcript, you stated that on the 23rd of October you were at the camp. I heard that in French. In English they used the word "camp," in French "campement," and I wondered: What is a civilian person doing in a military camp? Could you please tell me what you actually meant when you said that on the 23rd of October you were at the camp? Did you go there to meet friends, or can you shed some light on this, please?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to explain. The lady asked me this. She asked me -- well, it says there in this document that there were soldiers in Stupni Do, these reinforcements. How many did she say? One -- one platoon as reinforcement, which I can't confirm because on the 23rd I was in the camp. That's what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what would and civilian be doing in a military camp? What were you doing there? Because generally when you're speaking of military facilities, barracks, you don't find any civilians there. You only find military personnel. So what were you doing there?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all these were civilians, the ones who were with me. Esref was only -- well, for example, Mujo Cizmo was an elderly man. He was sort of -- about 60 years old, and he wasn't a member. There was Fahrija Balta. He was 60 or 70 years old. He wasn't a member either, and they were in that military camp or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But what would civilians be doing in a military camp? What are civilians doing in a military camp? That's what I'm trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. That's where we were brought. I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you were brought there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to clarify a point which was a bit ambivalent. There was talk about the defence of Stupni Do and mention of a platoon of 39 persons. Now, in the oral exchanges, one could get the impression that this platoon was a reinforcement, whereas the text in the document provided to us by Ms. Alaburic I read that the defence consisted of one reinforced platoon of 39 persons, and that would mean that this platoon was not a reinforcement but it was the defence. It was reinforced, but the whole defence consisted in one platoon with 39 men. Which is correct? Do you know, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that the second -- the latter part of what you said, that that was the unit from Stupni Do. That was that defence platoon or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's -- oh, yes. Ms. Alaburic wanted to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you please repeat for us, if I remember what it was that you stated yesterday, how many members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were there in Stupni Do? What did you say to us?

utterances.speaker: MUFID LIKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that it was about 20 men, but you know what, I mean, I cannot say exactly. Well, that's the way it was put. Approximately about 20 men. Now, was it 20 or more ...

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to draw your attention to what it was that the witness said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does the Prosecution have additional questions, redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, your testimony's now completed, sir. Thank you on behalf of the Bench, and have a good trip back home. Mr. Usher is going to take you out of the courtroom. We're going to lower the blinds because we have some protective measures for the next witness. No, no. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next Prosecution witness does not request any protective measures; is that right? Who is going to take the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I am, Your Honours, and I can confirm to you that at this point in time the witness did instruct us this morning that she is happy and comfortable to testify in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I had asked for this pause to just inform the Trial Chamber that my client wishes to be present. I'm told that other clients may also wish to be present during this hearing tomorrow. I know that this may pose a problem with the space, but also in looking at the agenda it would appear to me that perhaps the time that's being allotted may not be sufficient. The issues are relatively important. I would -- I would ask that the hearing be held either tomorrow afternoon when we're scheduled to hear witnesses or to hear it on Friday or to hear it on Monday for the -- so the Prosecution can make adjustments to their witnesses to be heard perhaps after Monday. But I think that the clients, at least my client wishes to be present, and I think this is not just a procedural issue. What might have been a procedural issue of a relatively minor nature months ago, I think now the issue is such that I think a full-blown hearing in a court such as this where all the clients are present may be more appropriate, and I believe that Mr. Murphy may wish to chime in on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to bring this discussion to an end. Mr. Karnavas took the floor whilst he didn't know of the points that we selected. Among such points there are only problems in connection with technical, forensic matters that have nothing to do with the case on the merits. If later on it turns out to be necessary for the accused to be present, we'll be open to the idea of a hearing with the accused, only if it is necessary, but since we're going to deal only with other matters than substantial matters that would -- those would require the presence of the accused, so it's not necessary here. Of course it's up to you to then convey to your clients what was said during the hearing. It may be that as of Monday already I might summarise the proceedings of tomorrow. Then we could have the accused in only if it is necessary. But right now we don't see the need for their presence. Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Let me not take up too much time, just a sentence. I think that, once, there should be a meeting held with the accused, too, because there are problems that affect us directly, of course. We are accused, and they are entitled to know what the facts are all about. I would like to present my own answer to the Trial Chamber to the last speech made by Mr. Scott, which I believe does not belong in a court of law, which is not right, and I need to respond to that. Saying things like, "this is expensive," "complicated," and what have you not. We all know that this is an expensive business, and we knew from day one what this was about, and so what are we talking about? Fishing. And so what they're trying to do is -- well, let's get this done. Let's behead these people. So if we do not complete something, if we do not clarify it, that is because we haven't got enough money. So these questions that appear here time and again, we don't have enough money, or we do have enough money, there's lots of paper, we cannot photocopy things, we cannot have them translated, and also, this last speech that was made, when he said he wanted the victims to be sitting here as well, that is not right for a court of law, and I'm sorry that the Judges did not react to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Praljak. We take due note of what you've just said. You have made a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Let me just -- for one or two seconds, if I may. It seems to me in view of what the -- clearly there's some feeling among the accused, and one has to be sensitive not only to actual fairness but to the appearance of fairness. And we are -- of course, we haven't had the advantage of seeing the final agenda, and I wonder if, Your Honour, we -- when that has been distributed, as I understand it's imminent, we could perhaps, at the end of the next witness, be given just a couple of minutes to come back to this question, if it appears to be necessary in the light of the agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy, again your words have been translated. They are in the transcript. I've taken note of what you've just said. Of course, the Prosecution has a right of reply. Very quickly, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to Your Honours and everyone. I would reiterate a point made earlier in the week by Mr. Scott in the more general context of allowing the parties to be heard, and if the Chamber would be inclined at all to moving the date of the hearing, I would, with all due respect, ask to be heard on that because I can assure the Trial Chamber that postponing or moving any of the witnesses in the next few days or weeks will be extremely problematic, given the distances that the witnesses are coming from. So I -- I would, with all due respect, insist that we be heard before the hearing tomorrow is moved to any time in the near future other than, I will telescope, the 23rd of April, when we don't have a witness scheduled. So that's all I wanted to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Rest assured the idea was never to postpone the hearing. We'll have a meeting tomorrow at 9.00 together with you, Mr. Scott, and your team, and also with the Defence counsel present here. You have an hour to say whatever you have to say, and depending on the points on the agenda, the Defence will have an hour to express their views, make their submissions. Then we are going to deliberate on the Bench, because the goal is to know what to do so that the questions put by the Judges do not harm the -- your case when you put questions to a witness. That's our objective. This is what we're trying to achieve, and if we can agree all together, so much the better. Of course, Mr. Praljak has just raised another problem. So has Mr. Murphy. Of course we are going to discuss this among Judges, and if we feel that it is necessary for Mr. Praljak, for Mr. Murphy, or for other people to make submissions, we will allow that of course. So rest assured, Mr. Praljak, what you have said has been taken into account and you will have an answer. We have a whole series of witnesses. We are going to have the first witness. For the next witness, I understood, but I may be wrong, that you are not going to need much time on the Prosecution side, as -- and the Defence had an hour and a half, according to the 65 ter list, but it may be that they don't use this entire time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, madam. Can you hear me? If you can hear me, it tell me that you understand what I say. Madam, you are being called as a witness by the Prosecution. You're going to make a solemn declaration, but first can you give me your name, first name, surname, and date of birth. No need to look at the screen unless you know English, but if you don't know English, it may confuse you. First name, surname, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Mufida Likic. I was born on the 1st of July, 1979.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Do you have a current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I work in the Vares-Majdan elementary school as a cleaner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you testified it previously before a court of law as to the events that took place in your country, or is this the first time that you're going to testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please stand up and read out the solemn declaration handed over to you by Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, madam. Please sit down. Some explanations. You are a witness pursuant to 92 ter proceedings. You're going to have a few questions by the Prosecution, and thereafter the Defence counsel and Judges may ask questions of you. The Defence might ask questions of you and the Judges might ask questions clarifying your written statement. If at any point you do not feel well, do not hesitate to ask for a break. If you do not understand the meaning of a question, there again do not hesitate to say so and ask the people asking the question to reformulate it, because what matters is the answer you give to a given question. So there it is. The floor is to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour. Good afternoon to Your Honours the Defence and everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And good afternoon, Ms. Likic. To start with, Your Honours, I will read a summary which is based on the 65 ter statement. The witness in this case was a Bosnian Muslim girl from Stupni Do who was 14 years old at the time of the attack. At the time, changes in the area began with policemen wear camouflage uniforms with Croatian Defence Council patches. The Croatian Defence Council stopped her many times and took her goods. Once she and a friend -- once she and a friend were told not to come back to Vares-Majdan --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Once she and a friend were told not to come to Vares-Majdan but to stay in her own village. On -- on the 23rd of October, 1993, at about 8.00 a.m., the witness heard shooting and the sound of a grenade. She hid with her family and some neighbours in their basement. After a while, they ran and hid in the basement of other neighbours. All together there were 13 persons including women and children. The witness saw smoke coming from her house and the stables in flames. The house of her Serb neighbour was also on fire. She saw men in black uniforms with a white band around their upper arms and baseball caps with a white U on them. When soldiers approached the house, the women tried to escape. The witness saw houses in the neighbourhood on fire. She also saw Merima Likic lying on the stairs of a neighbour's house with her two children Mebrura Likic and Vahidin Likic, who were huddled beneath her in the spaces between the landings and her body. She was just trying to protect them. The witness hid behind a metal barrel and felt something hit had the barrel. She realised she was shot in the leg. She made her way back to the basement of her neighbour where three other persons, her sister together with Hadzija Likic and Nevzeta Likic were located. They heard men's voices in the house calling out for anyone in the basement. The witness heard a round of gunfire and felt her sister's body get heavy on top of her. The three other women were shot and killed but the witness was protected by her sister's body. The witness was able to flee to the nearby woods but encountered soldiers in camouflage uniforms. As she ran away they began to shoot at her but she was able to escape. She climbed into a tree in the woods and hid. She could see Stupni Do and the surrounding hamlets and several houses were on fire. After about an hour she went back to town and hid with several other people in another basement of another neighbour. By now the shooting had stopped. At around 2.00 a.m., the people in the basement left and fled to the woods. After about two days, with the help of UNPROFOR, they were able to get to Dabravine. And that concludes the statement, the summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Ms. Likic, did you ever provide witness statements to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that you gave these statements on the 15th of March, 1996, and the 13th of October, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at those times that you provided these statements, did you answer the questions of the investigators truthfully?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you do so without any coercion or pressure?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: No pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at the conclusion of those interviews were your statements read back to you in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you remember did you sign each statement in the English language?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now when you travelled here to The Hague a few days ago, do you remember you met with myself and an investigator yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And were you given an opportunity of reading your two statements again?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And would it be true to say that the own correction that you had to make was to one statement in which you changed a name Likic to another name?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And so, do both of your statements now reflect what you would tell the Judges, had you to give evidence in full today?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, could I ask the witness firstly to be shown Prosecution Exhibit number 09884, bearing ERN number 00381926 to 1936.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Ms. Likic, if you would turn to the next document on that under the tab 9884, you will see a document in English in front you, and if you turn the pages you will see signatures on each page. Do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Whose signature is -- do you see?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: My signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And would you turn now to the next document in the booklet, which is 9885. And again you'll see in front of you a document in English, and again there's a signature. Would you again just look at the pages and tell me if you recognise the signatures? Do you recognise them? You won't see them on the other documents, just on the English document.

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Again is that your signature and initials?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, in both your statements given to the ICTY, you stated that on the 23rd of September the village was attacked and that you were hiding with others in a basement of a neighbour's house. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you tell the panel -- can you tell the panel about this basement? Can you describe it for us, how big it was? Was it small or big?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: No. It was a biggish basement. Well, I can only tell it you approximately. I don't know how to describe this. Well, people could live there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, sorry if I'm interrupting. I had a quick glance at the documents you intended to submit to the witness, and I saw that there were photographs among the documents with victims on them. I don't want to shock, you know, the witness again. If there is no objection from the Defence, it might not be necessary to show the witness the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. I'll ask her in a different manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: If I can just return to the basement for the moment. In terms of the basement, can you tell me how you would access to the basement? Was there a stairs or a step or a ladder?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: There were a few steps or stairs to the basement. There were two doors through which you entered that basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And was there a window in the basement?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: It had two small windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you know what the basement was used for?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, for winter supplies and other things, small things.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, do you remember yesterday when we met I showed you a photograph of a room from a set of photographs?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Was that the basement in which you were with other people on the 23rd of September?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: When we say the 23rd of September, what year are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: September?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: September -- I beg your pardon. 23rd of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Was this the 23rd of October rather than September.

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: We're talking of the month now, about October in what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you looked at the photograph, you identified it as the room, the basement in which you were held; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you also looked at the last photograph in the bundle of photographs, and do you remember that there was -- there was a cooker on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, do you remember if that cooker was present in the basement on the day you were there?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, and this part will be a little bit harder, and I'm sorry to have to -- to refer you to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Flynn, if you want to submit the photograph of the cooker, you can do so. That's not the problem. I was thinking about the other photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I know exactly what you were thinking, but I was afraid in looking through for the cooker one might stumble across the other photographs. Perhaps with the assistance of the usher --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: As we are -- as we are interrupted anyway. Witness, you have said that the picture you were shown was the picture in the basement in which you were, but you were in different basements, according to what you have told the Prosecutor. Is this basement the last basement in which you had been, or the first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but there was a fire-burning stove mentioned. There was the first basement and the second one where we were. So that house had actually two basements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It is the basement in which you found yourself before you ran away into the woods. Is it that one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can't speak for any other Defence counsel, but for -- on behalf of myself I don't require the witness to be shown any photographs at all. It will be quite satisfactory for the Prosecution to introduce them without reference to the witness, if Mr. Flynn chooses to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: What I'll do is I'll just read the ERN numbers and the exhibit numbers, and the e-court page numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: In any event, can you tell us who was in the basement with you on this day, this last basement in which you were hiding?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: I was there, my sister Medina was there, then my aunt Hatidza, and also Nevzeta Likic and her daughter Nerma Likic. And there was Melca Beganovic. There was -- I apologise. There was Merima Likic with her two children, Vahida, and Mebrura. There was Kada Likic and her son Adis Likic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did -- at some stage, did many of these ladies leave the basement and leave only you, your sister Hatidza and Nevzeta?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And at this time you four ladies were there, did either of you -- did any of you have a weapon amongst you of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: What kind of a weapon did you have?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: There was some sort of homemade rifle, if I can put it that way, and a bomb of some kind, but they took that away from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you said in your statement that you heard noises upstairs. You heard some shouting. You then heard a burst -- a burst of gunfire and that your body -- your sister's body became heavy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And you climbed out of a pit in the basement in which you were hiding and you shook the other ladies but it appeared that they were dead. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Did you see any wounds on the other three girls?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, in one of the photographs which you showed you yesterday there was a picture of three girls in the basement. Do you remember that? This was photograph --

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: -- 00357593. Did you recognise the people in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: My sister Medina, aunt Hatidza, and Nevzeta.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And I showed you another photograph which was number 00357599, which was more or less the same from a different angle. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And in the photographs we saw the three girls, and the girl on the right-hand side appeared to be wearing what appears to be a camouflage vest of some kind. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And this is the type of vest worn either by soldiers or by hunters. Could you tell the panel why this person -- why this girl was wearing this particular item of clothing on this particular day?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Because it was cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell us, was she a member of or did she have any direct connection with the ABiH defenders of the village?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. She was there. She worked in the kitchen for the village guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So she was a 14-year-old girl working in the kitchens. No other connection?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that she was in the kitchen. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, as you went through your statement, you told of escaping from the basement and passing through the village, seeing properties burned, and eventually you managed to make contact with your father. And in the second last page of the English version of your statement, you said that your father, the following night, went back into the village to see the dead bodies of your sister Hatidza and Nevzeta, and that he also came across the bodies of Merima, Mebrura, Vahidin, Lejla, Indira, and Adis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Were these people Merima Likic, Mebrura Likic, Vahidin Likic, Lejla Zutic Likic, Indira Zutic, and Adis Likic, whom you said in your statement had been with you earlier in the basement before the killing?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, after the Stupni Do attack, do you know if there was any examination carried out on the bodies of the people killed in Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Would you kindly repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: I was wondering that -- if you knew whether -- after the attack on Stupni Do, whether you knew if any examination was carried out on the bodies of the people that were killed, any medical examinations.

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. All I know is that they went to Visoko for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you know of death certificates at a later stage issued in respect of each person that was killed?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Have you ever seen a death certificate for your sister Medina?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could I ask you to look at Exhibit 8659. This is a stamped certain of death issued by Vares municipality on the 19th of March, 1996, containing a stamp of the municipality and signed by someone with the name Taib Ahmis. Do you know that person, Taib Ahmis?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Well, have a look at the certificate. We have a certificate issued in the name of Medina Likic, date of birth 9th of April, 1972. Father's name Likic Sulejman, and mother's name Mevla Osmanovic. Is that your sister from those details?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Before I ask you to look at another one, can you tell me -- can you give me some details in relation to the other lady in the basement, Hatidza? Can you tell me the name of her father and mother?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Salko Likic and Zlatka Likic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So if I ask you to turn to document 8661 on your bundle, if you go to the tab on the end -- at the edge of the page, and find 8661, towards the back -- do you have it?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher again.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: So on this document, you have a document issued at the top of the page Hatidza Likic, born 15 December 1950 -- 42 and father and mother's name Salko Likic and Likic Zlatka. Is that the Hatidza who was in the basement with you and who was killed?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And would you tell me now the other girl that was in the basement, Nevzeta, did you tell me if she was married?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And do you know the name of her husband, and do you know the name of her father and mother?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names, please? Her husband's name.

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Jakub Likic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And her mother and father?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Rifet Islamovic and Hasnija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could I ask you to turn to document 8656. And again you'll have a certificate. It says Nevzeta Likic at the top. Date of birth, 18th of May, 1965. Jakub Likic husband and father and mother Rifet and Hasnija Islamovic. Is that the same Nevzeta who was in the basement with you?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, during our meeting yesterday, do you remember that we went through this exercise with a number of other death certificates and that you also gave me the names of either the husband, or the husband and the father and mother, in respect of Merima Likic, Mebrura Likic, Vahidin Likic, Lejla Zutic Likic, Indira Zutic, and Adis Likic before looking at the certificate of death issued in their names? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you confirm here today to the trial panel that the information or details that you gave me corresponded with the death certificates which I showed you?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have these other six death certificates, but to save time, and obviously with the approval of my colleagues on the Defence, I'm hoping that the Defence might be prepared to admit the -- and stipulate as to the contents, reserving the right of course to file any objection in writing. Each certificate has a similar signature and stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe there won't be any objections from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we certainly know -- have no objections, and I take it from the silence that I do speak for my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now at -- at page 00381931 of the English version of your statement to the ICTY, this is the first statement which you gave, you told you had been struck by a bullet when you were hiding behind a barrel. Can you tell Your Honours, where did this bullet strike you? I don't think you need -- you need look at it at all.

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: It grazed me on the left side of my left leg, and it hit me near the -- near my spine.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could I ask you to stand up, if you would, and if you could just demonstrate for Your Honours where, firstly, the bullet hit you, and then where the bullet came out. If you could just point to the entry location and then point to the exit location. So starting with the entry location. For the record, the witness is pointing to just above the belt-line on her back on the left-hand side. And if you could show us then where the bullet came out. The bullet came out just below the hip on the leg on the left-hand side. Thank you, you can sit down now again. After reaching Dabravine did you receive medical treatment for your wound?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And did you have to be hospitalised?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: How long did you spend in hospital?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: One month.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Why was it that you had to spend this length of time in hospital?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Because my wound became infected.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And after a month, were you released and were you able to go home?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Now, do you have any side-effects as a result of the wounds sustained by you on this day? Today, do you have any side-effects?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Could you tell Your Honours what side-effects you have?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Mostly when the weather changes. That's when I feel the side-effects most. I can't sleep. I feel some nervousness, and my leg hurts from the wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: That's it, Your Honour. I don't have any further questions for the witness. Just to -- for the completion of the record, I wanted to mention the e-court numbers for the photographs which I mentioned. 00357616, which is a photograph -- the first photograph of the room, e-court reference 130. The second photograph was of the cooker, 00357618, e-court reference 132. And the photographs of the bodies which I referred to, ERN number 00357624, e-court reference 138; 00357593, e-court reference 107; 00357599, e-court reference 113. And all of those photographs form part of a collection under Exhibit number P 06116. I don't know whether I should for the record stipulate -- I think I've given the exhibit numbers for each of the death certificates and that should be sufficient. And lastly, the two statements given will be tendered under seal. Actually -- actually, a correction on that. Since the witness has given evidence in open session, they don't need to be under seal any more. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The time has come for us to take the break. It is 20 to 4.00. We will have a 20-minute break and we will resume the proceedings in 20 minutes sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I now give the floor to the Defence. Mr. Karnavas, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President; good afternoon, Your Honours. We have no questions for this witness. We'd like to thank her for coming here to give her evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. Madam, I just have a few questions. I think we'll be over in about 10 minutes, the cross-examination will be over, but tell me, to start off with, do you remember how many inhabitants there were in Stupni Do in 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many inhabitants there were in the village on the day of the attack, on the 23rd of October, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge of the fact that civilians in the village left the village prior to the attack, one or two days before, a few days before the attack?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that one of your -- well, was it relatives, cousins, or was it somebody from the same village cooked for the village watch. Now, tell me, were there other women in the village and who had some task like that for the army, for the soldiers in the village itself?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: There were two other women, but I don't remember them very well. I don't know their names, and I don't know exactly anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, do you know in Stupni Do there was a unit belonging to the BH army there, a BH army unit?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: No. I was a child, and I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your statement you mention that your father was a member of the village watch or village guard, and you also said that there were some 50 young people who were also in the village watch. Can you confirm that? Is that correct or was that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The people that you mentioned, those 50-odd people in the village watch, they weren't members of the BH army, or am I wrong there?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, there were old people there, too, old men. They weren't all members of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that some of them were members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many of them perhaps were members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I was underage at the time. I was a minor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, in your statement you say that your father left the basement in order to defend the village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the other people were in order to defend the village?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, I think they were round about the village, around the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, now, around village, were there any trenches or fortifications which were supposed to serve for the village's defence?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, were any of them in any of the houses of the village and defended the village in that way?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You told us today in response to a question from my learned friend of the Prosecution, when asked whether you were armed, the four of you ladies who were in the basement, and your answer was that you had a rifle and a bomb but that that was confiscated, taken away from you. Can you explain when that rifle and that bomb were taken from you?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: When a member of the HVO came by. I didn't see that because I was hidden. I was hiding. But I heard it and I felt it when he came to us. I could hear that. And I heard what I said. He said that one of these women had a rifle and a bomb, and he said that he told her to give them up to him, and she handed that over to him. And I know nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And that soldier then left the basement, did he?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to ask you to clarify one more contradiction that appears in your two statements with respect to the events when you were fleeing the village and taking to the woods. In the first statement you've said, literally, and I'll quote you, it's on page 7 of the Croatian version of the statement, and in the English there are no page numbers, at least not the pages I have, so for Their Honours I will give the ERN number. It is 00381932. And you say there that you encountered that group of 15 soldiers, approximately 15 soldiers. That's what I'm going to refer to. You said you saw about 15 soldiers wearing black uniforms sitting or standing around Zineta Likic's house. "They were looking at in my direction and they could see me but they didn't stop me. They were talking but I wasn't able to hear their voices because of the distance. I continued running between the trees and I reached a path that was a curving path." And I'm going to stop there. Of course the text does go on. Now, in the second statement referring to this same event, on page 3 of the Bosnian version and on page 2 of the English text. You say: "When I left the village I noticed about 15 HVO soldiers in black uniforms standing around the house of Zineta Likic. Then I heard one of them -- then I heard somebody ordering these soldiers to run after me and to kill me. They started shooting at me, but I managed to escape them." Now, since the Prosecution in the summary of your statement just took your statement from the second statement, could you explain to us whether you told the truth when you gave the first statement or is the truth what you said in your second statement?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: The truth is what I said in the second statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, next. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. General Praljak just asked for permission to put one question. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Madam Witness. You said that to the best of your knowledge on the basis of what you heard from your father, there were around 50 people who were on the village watch; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I can't remember. I was a little girl then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: On page 3 of your statement I'm going to read out what you said: "There were many younger people who were on guard duty. I think there were about 50 of them. I say around 50 because I heard my father talking about these things to my mother and our relatives, Jakub and Esref Likic." These are your words. Are they correct?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure about that. I mean I said that in my statement, but since I was a minor at the time -- perhaps it was true, but I think it is true after all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Do you know that village guards, when they return from duty, go back home to have lunch or something like that, whereas these people, according to what you've said and what other people said, had a kitchen where three people were employed? Do you know that, after returning from their duty, people would go to a common room where there would be cooked meals provided for them like for the military?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want to have a redirect examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Just one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Witness, just on that question that General Praljak asked you. You said in your statement when referring to the number, "About 50, I think," and the 50 was based on what you heard your father say. Did you or do you remember, or did you ever see and count 50 members of the defence together anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: I did not have an opportunity to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: And can you say with absolute certainty that it was the number 50 that you heard your father talking about?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLYNN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. On behalf of the Trial Chamber I thank you for coming to testify in The Hague as to the events that are part of your written statement. I wish you a good return home. The usher is now going to take you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the next witness, there are protective measures, aren't there? Who is going to be taking the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, there are protective measures, and I'll be taking the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to move to closed session. Roll down the blinds.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: In summary of this witness's evidence, the witness is a Bosnian Muslim woman from Stupni Do and gives details of the attack on Stupni Do on the 23rd of October, 1993. At around 8.00 in the morning, the witness heard the sound of a shell exploding. She stayed in the house for a while and then went to a shelter joining several other villagers who were already there. They heard shooting from all directions. A villager came to the shelter and told them to run away because Croat soldiers were approaching the house. They tried to escape but only three succeeded and most of them came back to the shelter. A soldier wearing a white ribbon on his arm kicked down the door of the basement. He told the villagers to get out. The witness was one of the first to get out. She saw a woman from the village coming in their direction with soldiers. When they came out, she saw about 20 soldiers all in camouflage uniforms and with weapons. They separated the men from the women and asked for money, jewellery, and weapons. A soldier with an HVO patch grabbed the witness by the arm. The witness saw how one soldier cut the throat of a man named Edin Mahmutovic. The HVO soldiers forced the witness inside a house and there one of them raped her. Afterwards, the soldiers brought her out of the house and set it on fire. The witness then saw two bodies lying on the ground, one of whom was Edin Mahmutovic. The witness also witnessed the killing of another person, and soldiers then forced the witness and other villagers into a summer house, locked it, and set it on fire. The villagers were able to escape. During that night an old Muslim woman who had stayed with them died. The group stayed in the forest for a couple of days and then were taken by UNPROFOR to Dabravine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, may I say something? There is a mistake here in the name. Likic Rifet was cut by a knife, not Edin Mahmutovic. He was killed later. So Likic Rifet was the one who was wounded in the neck area with a knife. I just need to correct that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. That is of course a summary of the evidence, but nonetheless my apologies for any mistake that has been made in that. That concludes the summary of the evidence, and I'm now move to the formal procedure for the admission of two statements. Witness, do you remember being interviewed on two occasions by somebody from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that those occasions were the 4th of February, 1996, and the 28th of October, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And on those occasions, did you answer the questions put to you truthfully?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Only the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And did you do so voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Now, on both of those occasions, at the end of the interview, do you recall the statements being read back to you in your own language?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And do you recall then signing each of those statements that had been prepared to confer --

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: -- confirming that they were true to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown in the exhibits bundle Exhibits 9913 and 9914.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Witness, you'll see in front of you both an English and then following that a B/C/S version of the statements. Have you had the opportunity to read these statements since coming to The Hague to give your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And by looking at both of these statements, are you able to confirm that your initials appear on each of the pages of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Having re-read these statements, and as you went through and -- when we met yesterday, I understand that you had some minor corrections to make to the 1996 statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: And in the interests of saving time, those corrections were put together and forwarded to the Defence and the Chamber. I hope they've received those corrections that were made in the proofing session. Witness, having made those corrections, do you stand by the contents of both of your statements as being true to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: MUFIDA LIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GILLETT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be tendering both of those statements in due course under seal in light of the detail contained in the statements and the substantial number of names that are mentioned. Your Honour, I now have a number of exhibits to put to this witness, and Your Honour will no doubt see from the exhibit list that the vast majority concern death certificates, and by their very nature, involving the names that they do and the questions that I will ask the witness in order that she is able to identify the persons prior to being shown the documents, it may be prudent if we could pass into private session in order to avoid names being mentioned that may identify the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I won't need to mention the gentleman's name, but needless to say --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at it from a practical standpoint because I think we need to be speaking on the same language. First of all, we're talking about hundreds of pages of handwritten notes that this gentleman took while he was along with the two negotiators, primary negotiators where he, one, recounts what he observes and then, two, he has his personal notes which are rather telling, which is he's making characterisation who he thinks is lying, who he thinks is obstructing, who is reneging, and so on and so forth. These are actual notes that you see. When you look at the volume of all of this material, from a practical standpoint it's virtually impossible for a lawyer to sit there with his client in the -- at the UNDU at this stage of the proceedings to go over all of this. It's just -- it is. It's impractical. Even if you were -- had access for a week, it would take longer than that. And I know that because I've -- I've studied these -- these documents, and they're voluminous and they're very tedious.
