From a translation standpoint, just to let you know, the challenges that we face with this institution when it comes to translation, okay, because the UN is great when it comes to human rights in a general sense, but when it comes to human rights, applying it, the UN itself to it's own institutions, I dare say they fall rather short at times. The policy here is you need to know exactly what you're going to be putting to the witness in order to get that translated. Now, think about it. And of course the people who are making these decisions have never tried a case, nor do they know what a lawyer has to go through to choose whether it's the Prosecution or the Defence, what exactly they're going to put to the witness at that particular moment. Let's just say we knew we had that magic ball and we were able to determine exactly what we needed to put before the witness. It would take literally months. The paperwork that you have to fill, and they're back-logged. We're talking literally months. To get funding, private funding that -- there is some available for the Defence, they will not use that. They will not provide it to the Defence because they don't consider that necessary. They will only provide translation funding if you have a language problem between your -- with you and your client and you need to translate it to communicate with, because some foreigners don't have access -- don't speak the language. So that's the -- so from an institutional point of view getting it translated in advance, it's impossible unless you have a cache of money, private funding, that you can do that. With respect to this particular witness, I just want to make sure that the Trial Chamber fully understands who we're talking about, because if you look at the -- if you look at the indictment, we're talking about this joint criminal enterprise that takes place from 1991 to 1994. The Prosecution is actually going a year, even earlier and a year later, although probably I wouldn't -- it wouldn't surprise me if they think it's still going on. But be that as it may, the reason why these notebooks are so critical is because they go all the way up until before the Washington Agreement. But, you see, you have to look at all of them in order to get a full picture, and you can't look at what happened in Krajisnik or what happened in Milosevic because those were different negotiations. They were minor in comparison to what we're talking about. And because of the scope of the indictment, I think it's necessary to look at all of it because then you can fully understand Croatia, for instance. What role is Croatia playing? Because you can see that Tudjman is being engaged by the international community to assist. They say he's involved in the joint criminal enterprise because he's engaged. The negotiators, however, are engaging him as part of the process. Croatia has its problems with Milosevic and Serbia. They say there is this Karadjordjevo. Nobody attended. Everybody knows what happens, though. So there you have Milosevic playing his games with Croatia. Croatia is occupied, one-third of it is gone basically. It's in control. They're claiming at the same time while Serbia is occupying Croatia Tudjman and Milosevic are planning to carve up Bosnia. And that's why you need to look at all of this in order to get a flavour of what is happening. I dare say in my opinion thus far he's probably the most important witness with respect to this -- this big global picture. So I think -- I think that Your Honours may want to rethink a little bit this issue about translation, because I think that a client, an accused, is entitled to assist in his own defence even if he has a lawyer. I won't belabour the point. As far as the hours are concerned. I'm not sure 10 hours is enough. We're going to discuss that tomorrow not with respect to this particular witness but I probably will have some things to say how we feel, we the Defence feels that the amount of time allocated to us is based on -- on the Prosecution and not based on what our needs are. In other words, they dictate the agenda for you to dictate to us. They say they need four hours and you come up with a formula. Sometimes it's four, sometimes it's five, sometimes it's six hours, but nonetheless we think that we need to be heard on some critical witnesses. It's unfortunate that Mr. Bozidar Kovacic isn't here. He's sick, otherwise I would ask that we proceed with the hearing today, but I don't think it would be fair to Mr. Praljak. Finally my client indicated to me during the break that he wished to say something to the Trial Chamber with respect to attending. I think he should be given an opportunity. I think he wants to speak and he wants to speak for maybe 30 seconds, that's all. And he rarely says anything, so I think he should be heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. Mr. Karnavas, just a few words, but your client wants to take the floor, so I'll give the floor to Mr. Prlic. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: [Interpretation] I'd like to say good afternoon. As you know, I don't always intervene, and I don't wish to take part for my own reasons and my own principles in the meritus, but I have to intervene sometimes. I received a proposed agenda for the meeting tomorrow and with all due respect I have to say these are not only procedural matters that are on the agenda and therefore I would like to ask you to perhaps rethink your ruling and decision to allow me and the other accused who wish to attend to attend the meeting that we're going to have tomorrow, because I think that there are important questions not only questions of principle but questions of substance as well which are very decisive when it comes to this -- these proceedings. And this is the third request that we have made and that you have refused. The first thing I asked for was a laptop so as to be able to keep my notes and I spoke to the Deputy Registrar and he said that personally he had nothing against that. I asked for more time with a witness; that was rejected too. And the position of my Defence counsel is quite clear and known. My Defence team has just a sixth of the time compared to the Prosecution at this stage of the trial. And, finally, my third point this is perhaps just a technical matter and that is why I would like to ask you to reconsider your decision or to rethink it and give a positive answer, that I can follow the way in which decisions are made regarding my fate. Thank you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the question of the relationship between this type of accused and their counsel is a very complicated one. It's a question of knowledge, cognisance, and so on. Now, I took part in everything that led to the democratic elections taking place in Croatia. My Defence counsel did not. I took part in a very narrow circle of people, and so they cannot recognise in a document that they happen to be reading something that I can readily recognise as being important. Let me give you an example. When you send out a very good lawyer or mathematician to a forest, they don't see that the forest is suffering from some sickness. So, Your Honours, by the same token you can't talk to somebody about a hundred pages, for instance, of Marcel Proust on the scent and of -- or the odour of cakes, but the wonderful Defence counsel that I have, that is representing me, cannot recognise in a document of this kind what a request means whether the Croats in Posavina did something to the Muslims or whatever. I cannot instruct him in all the brigades, units, hills, and dales of the configuration of the land. That is impossible in this type of proceedings. I'm sorry to have to say that, but I'm afraid of things being reduced, greatly reduced in something that is called society in general, and from Saint-Simone and sociology and Auguste Comte and so on, society represents something which to the present day finds it very hard to find answers to why, with all the good intent in the world that we all have, ugly things happen all over the world. And then what the responsibility and accountability of individuals are, and my own accountability too. So faced with an indictment of this kind which covers such a long period of time and such complex social situations, the political games that are being played, you necessarily have to give people a chance and I'm speaking about myself now here to try and provide Your Honours with an answer for you to be able to weigh up the evidence in the end and whether actions of one kind merit a sentence and, if so, what kind of sentence should be meted out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I am aware of time and the need, I believe, to take a break if we're going to continue it, either recess for the evening or continue, but let me just say two points very quickly about the Okun diaries and the need for translations thereof. As I pointed out yesterday, these diaries have been the subject of admission into evidence in at least three other cases before this Tribunal and in none of those cases has any Trial Chamber ever ordered the full translation of those diaries, and again these other cases also have involved very senior level political and/or military leaders. Second. Second, as Mr. Karnavas indicated yesterday, and I don't know perhaps if this was an error in the transcript or the translation, perhaps, but on pages 78 and 79 of yesterday's hearing, Mr. Karnavas indicated that he would be tendering into evidence all of the diaries at which point it would seem that the logical way to proceed in that event would be, in effect, that would constitute a waiver of the right of the accused to have those diaries in their own language if the Defence is unable to produce one. If a Defence counsel stands up and tenders hundreds of pages of material that's not available in a language that the accused understands, then that right is being waived at least with respect to that one Defence team, if, in fact, they're unable to get -- for resource reasons to get those materials translated. If Mr. Karnavas has already decided that they're all relevant and that they all need to come in, then that one possible avenue would be to consider that a waiver of the right to have that material presented because, of course, a Defence team or an accused or can waive many of the rights that exist in criminal proceedings. I will leave it at that because of time constraints. I'm not sure if Chambers wants further submissions on this or on any of the other issues that have been -- that have arisen, but I am also aware of the fact that we're rapidly to the point where we need to either adjourn or a recess because of the need to change the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honour. The first point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute, Mr. Karnavas. I'll give you the floor later on. Let me just say a few words. It seems to me, but I don't have the specific references to the Trial Chamber or Appeals Chamber's decisions I'm thinking of, but I believe as for translations that when an accused person, whatever his language, when an accused person is represented by counsel, the Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that these documents should be provided either in English or in French. I believe that's well-established case law at this Tribunal. However, when you have an accused defending himself, if memory serves me right it's -- we have Seselj and Milosevic who did that, then in that case the accused is entitled to receive the documents in his own mother-tongue. As for the Milosevic, and I followed what was going on in that case, of course, as everyone else, apparently the diary that we are talking about, the ambassador diary, was provided to him in English. I'm not sure. Some of the passages might have been translated into his own language and he and he organised his cross-examination on the basis of what he receive. That's all I can say. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as Milosevic goes, first, he didn't recognise the Tribunal although he showed up to the court every day, and he had an armada of staff working for him behind the scenes as well, helping him out. Plus, he read English very well and spoke English. He ad worked in the United States and, of course, during the negotiations, they were done in English as far as I understand. But getting back to Mr. Mundis's two arguments, first, the first one is not an argument to say, well, it was admitted -- the diaries were admitted in part in three other trials and therefore none of the Trial Chambers requested that they be translated and therefore it's not necessary in this case. First of all, I don't know what if any requests were made in those other cases. That's number one. Number two, Mr. Praljak, as well as others, are heavily engaged in assisting in their own defence by -- by reading the documents and going over them with their clients, and I dare say that an accused is entitled to be able to read documents in his own language particularly when they go to a critical aspect of the case. But in any event, I think the first argument is -- is not much of an argument. As far as the second argument that Mr. Mundis said, i don't -- I'm unaware of any jurisprudence, now, maybe there's some out there and Mr. Mundis is very bright and writes quite a bit about the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. Perhaps he could cite us some -- some jurisprudence. It says that once I tender the document in its entirety, there is some sort of a waiver. I'm unaware of that. No, if he -- what he meant to say was, it could be viewed as a waiver, I think that's open to debate. But as far as whether in fact it is a waiver I'm unaware of any jurisprudence and of course shame on me if I'm ignorant of the case law but if there is some case law I certainly would like to look it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Two points very quickly. I believe what I said or what I intended to say, at least, was it could be constituted or construed as a waiver; as any virtually any other right can be waived, the right to remain silent is waived when an accused takes the stand. The right to receive material in the language the accused understands can be waived if that accused's counsel tenders that material without having it in the language the accused understands, and that could be construed or constituted as a waiver. Let me say one other point though about the material that the Prosecution has placed on the exhibit list that comes from the Okun diaries, because I wasn't want there to be any confusion about this. Those excerpts which are on the Prosecution list that come from Ambassador Okun's diaries have been translated into the language of the accused or is in the process of being translated into the language of the accused. We are not talking about tendering into evidence excerpts from the diaries which have not been translated. The issue here is whether there's some requirement to translate those remaining portions of the diary which the Prosecution is not intending to use, and our position is: If the Defence wants to use those remaining parts, then they have an obligation to get those parts translated or, if they want to use them without the benefit of having them all fully translated, that could be construed as a waiver of the right of the accused to have that material in their own language. But I want to be very clear that what we're talking about is excerpts from the diaries, those excerpts will be available in the language of the accused when they are tendered into evidence at the hearings involving Ambassador Okun.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Listen, we have to take a break now. There are only a few minutes of tape left. The Judges need to consider these matters immediately, because we might be able to find a solution that is agreeable to everyone, but we need to discuss this. It's 10 to 6.00. We'll resume at 10 past 6.00 for a very short time, but we will resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The hearing is resumed. Let me first give the floor to the registrar because he has a few IC numbers to give us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Just very briefly. OTP has submitted a list of documents to be tendered through Witness DG. The list shall be given the Exhibit number IC 502. OTP has also submitted a list of documents to be tendered through Witness Mufid Likic. This list shall be given Exhibit number IC 503. And finally, OTP has submitted a list of documents to be tendered through Witness Mufida Likic. This list shall be given Exhibit number IC 504. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. During the break that took slightly longer than I expected, the Judges considered the two issues raised by the Defence. The first point was related to the presence of the accused persons in the courtroom when we deal with the issues in the agenda that was handed out to the parties this afternoon, and the second point was related to the issue of the translation of the diaries, of the entire diaries of Ambassador Okun. First oral decision related to the presence of the accused persons in the courtroom to take part in the hearing. The Trial Chamber stands by the decision it has already taken. In other words, tomorrow in Courtroom II at 9.00 a.m., a hearing will be held under Rule 65 ter with the Prosecution and Defence counsel. Tomorrow the Prosecution will have one hour to make their submissions, and the Defence will also have 60 minutes. In order to respond to the request made by the accused, we've decided that as quickly as possible, in the next few days, we'll have a hearing dedicated to the same issue, and during that hearing the accused persons will be able to take the floor in order to tell us in individually, if they wish to do so, what their point of view is, but we need to specify that beforehand they will have been informed by Defence counsel who will notify them of what was said at the hearing that will take place tomorrow morning. In other words, we grant the request made by the accused persons. They will participate but another day and as quickly as possible. If a witness does not show up, for example, we'll do it immediately because it will take about one hour, or, alternatively, we'll hold an additional hearing if the schedule allows us to do so. So rest assured, gentlemen, we will listen to you. This is the first decision. Second oral ruling, it relates to the translation of the documents from Ambassador Okun's personal diaries. After having heard the Defence, Mr. Praljak, Mr. Prlic, as well as the Prosecution in the person of Mr. Mundis, after deliberating on that point the Trial Chamber has decided to maintain the decision it had taken with respect to the translation of the documents. We've already read out paragraphs 4 to 5 of the decision, and I'd like to refer you to that decision. That settles the issue according to us. We do not intend to alter, to modify the decision in any way, and this decision was taken by the Judges unanimously. It's a quarter past 6.00. The hearing stands adjourned. We'll reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.00 a.m., with the Prosecution and Defence counsel, and tomorrow afternoon at 2.15 we'll reconvene yet again with the accused present for the next witness. Thank you very much.
